opus-5.5.text:
What I find really interesting is that cryptography papers sit at this unusual intersection. On one hand they're very mathematical: there are definitions, reductions, security proofs. On the other hand, the writing conventions in crypto are quite different from what you'd see in, say, a number theory or algebra paper. A lot of the arguments are game-based, there are probabilistic statements, asymptotic notions like "negligible," and a fair amount of what I'd call "standard hand-waving," steps that the community agrees are routine, so nobody writes them out.

When you ask a prover to turn that into Lean, all of that implicit knowledge has to become explicit. You can't just say "by a standard hybrid argument." You have to actually define the hybrids, state what the adversary has access to, and pin down exactly what is being quantified over. So the formalization process becomes a kind of stress test of the paper itself. Sometimes you discover that a definition was slightly underspecified, or that two sections were using a term in subtly different ways, and the system forces you to resolve that.

The second thing I find exciting is the infrastructure question. Mathlib is very strong in areas like algebra and analysis, but the foundations for cryptographic reasoning, things like probability over adversaries, oracle access, computational indistinguishability, are much less developed. So part of the work is the prover not just proving a theorem but also building up or reusing the right abstractions along the way. That's a much more realistic picture of what mathematical research looks like: you're not only filling in proofs inside an existing library, you're also deciding what the right definitions should be.

And then, more philosophically, crypto is one of those fields where correctness really matters in the real world. A subtle flaw in a security proof can translate into a broken protocol that people actually deploy. So if AI-assisted formal verification can make it cheaper to get machine-checked guarantees for these proofs, that's not just a nice demo for mathematicians. It's potentially something with real practical value. To me, that's a glimpse of where this technology goes: from proving olympiad problems to helping verify the kinds of arguments society actually depends on.

fable-5.1.text:
What I found most interesting is that cryptography is one of the few areas of mathematics where the gap between "we believe this is true" and "we have actually checked every step" has real consequences. A security proof in a paper might be twenty pages long, written by very smart people, reviewed by other very smart people, and still contain a subtle error in how a reduction handles some edge case. Those errors have historically gone unnoticed for years. So when we took a cryptography paper and had Axiom work through it in Lean, the exciting part wasn't just that it could formalize the definitions. It was watching where it got stuck.

Every place the prover struggled turned out to be a place where the paper was doing something informal. The author would write "by a standard hybrid argument" or "the adversary's advantage is clearly negligible," and a human reader nods along because they've seen that pattern a hundred times. But Lean doesn't nod along. It asks: which hybrid, exactly? What's the bound? Where does the negligibility come from? And in forcing those questions, you discover that the "standard" argument sometimes needs an extra assumption the paper never stated, or that two definitions that look equivalent on the page actually differ in a way that matters for the theorem.

The other thing I find compelling is the scale question. Formalizing a paper like this by hand used to take a team of experts months. The definitions alone, things like probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries, indistinguishability games, these are notoriously annoying to encode faithfully. So very little cryptography has ever been formally verified, even though it's exactly the field where you'd most want it. If a system like Axiom can do most of that work, and a human only needs to step in to clarify what the author actually meant, then formal verification stops being a luxury for a handful of landmark results and becomes something you could do for the proofs that protect real systems.

And honestly, there's a nice feedback loop for the prover itself. Cryptography proofs are long, structured, and unforgiving about details. They're a great stress test. When the model learns to carry a complex reduction through fifty intermediate lemmas without losing track of what it's bounding, that's a kind of mathematical discipline that transfers to everything else we want it to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes Axiom and Lean checking formalized proofs, but does not say that someone who does not understand cryptography can establish an article’s correctness by obtaining a successful check.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that you’re taking an argument written for humans and making every step precise enough for a computer to check. In cryptography, a proof can depend on subtle assumptions about what an adversary can do or how a probability is bounded. Turning that into Lean forces you to spell those assumptions out.

The exciting question with the Axiom prover is how much of that translation it can help with. Can it bridge the gap between the article’s mathematical explanation and the formal definitions and lemmas you need? You still have to make sure the formal statement captures what the author intended. But if you get that right, you have something you can check, build on, and reuse.

r001.rationale: The response says Lean can check a formalization and stresses that it must capture the author’s intent, but it does not say that someone who does not understand cryptography can establish the article’s correctness from a successful check.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that translating a cryptography article into Lean forces you to make every assumption explicit. In a paper, you might say that a step follows from a standard argument, and a knowledgeable reader fills in the details. A formal proof has to supply those details, and Lean checks that they actually fit together.

With the Axiom prover, the exciting question is how much of that translation we can automate: can it identify the right definitions, break an argument into useful lemmas, and produce proofs that Lean accepts? The goal is to capture the mathematical claim faithfully. In cryptography, where a security argument can depend on subtle assumptions, that seems particularly valuable.
